idiom_name: service module of coarse functions (class only for state or injected collaborators) with the ORM's atomic block as the unit of work
implementation_notes: A module of functions replaces the classic facade class: services/orders.py imports the fine-grained repositories and exposes one function per use case, and the module name plus its function names are the public surface, so no interface has to be declared. Transaction demarcation comes from the persistence framework rather than from a container - @transaction.atomic (Django) or with session.begin(): (SQLAlchemy) wraps the whole workflow in one unit of work, which is the direct analogue of the container-managed transaction. Keep the class form when the facade needs injected collaborators (constructor injection through a factory or a DI library) or per-conversation state; a bare module that reaches for a module-level session is the trap, not the idiom.
code_sketch:
# services/orders.py - the only import surface for the API layer
from django.db import transaction
from . import inventory, orders, pricing

@transaction.atomic                          # unit of work for the whole use case
def place_order(*, customer_id: str, sku: str, qty: int) -> str:
    q = pricing.quote(sku, qty)
    inventory.reserve(sku, qty)
    return orders.insert(customer_id, q, qty)   # commit/rollback decided by atomic

# SQLAlchemy alternative: with session.begin(): ... ; SQLModel/async variants wrap the
# same three calls in one session.begin() block.
pitfalls: Catching DatabaseError inside an atomic block hides the failure from Django's commit/rollback decision and can raise TransactionManagementError; catch outside the block instead.
A module-level Session/connection or global cache is shared by every request in a WSGI/ASGI worker; create the session per call or scope it to the framework's request.
ATOMIC_REQUESTS wraps the view, not the workflow: middleware and template rendering run outside the transaction, so it does not replace the facade's own boundary.
